According to investigators, the men allegedly approached them while posing as policemen and threatened them.
Police later examined CCTV footage from areas around the park and checked call detail records to trace the movements of the accused following the incident.
Investigators said Asif left after learning that police were searching for him. The two brothers allegedly went to a restaurant before returning to their home in Sri Niwaspuri.

The Supreme Court has reinforced safeguards against arbitrary arrest. Police must follow constitutional procedures and respect personal liberty before depriving anyone of freedom
Arrest law

Constituent Assembly member Somnath Lahiri, during a debate on 29 April 1947, made a striking remark that continues to resonate even 76 years after the enactment of the Indian Constitution, particularly in the context of the never-ending and often arbitrary exercise of the power of detention by the police. Lahiri said that the fundamental rights provisions in the Constitution had been drafted “from the point of view of a police constable”. He remarked:
“These are fundamental rights from a police constable’s point of view and not from the point of view of a free and fighting nation. Here, whatever right is given is taken away by a proviso.”

Whether it was the first constitutional case decided by the Supreme Court, concerning the preventive detention of Communist leader A.K. Gopalan, or one of India’s most consequential constitutional cases, _ADM Jabalpur_, the history of constitutional rights in India has repeatedly confronted the extraordinarily broad and, at times, arbitrary powers exercised by the police and the State.
## Individual Versus The State

How helpless an individual can be when confronted by the might of the State and its coercive machinery can perhaps be gauged from a question Justice H.R. Khanna posed to the then Attorney-General, Niren De, during the Habeas Corpus case. Justice Khanna asked whether, “if a police officer, because of personal enmity, killed another man, would there be any remedy?”

Justice Khanna, in his autobiography _Neither Roses, Nor Thorns_, recalled the answer of the Attorney-General as unequivocal: “Consistently with my argument,” he said, “there would be no judicial remedy in such a case as long as the Emergency lasts.” He added: “It may shock your conscience; it shocks mine, but consistently with my submissions, no proceedings can be taken in a court of law on that score.”

The exchange captures, in stark terms, the extraordinary vulnerability of an individual when the power to arrest and detain is placed beyond meaningful judicial scrutiny. More than seven decades after Lahiri’s warning, the question remains as relevant as ever: how do we ensure that the power of the State to deprive an individual of liberty does not become a licence for arbitrary arrest?
## Recent Arrest Raises Constitutional Questions

The contemporary relevance of this concern is evident in a recent judgment of the Supreme Court. A Bench comprising Justice Ujjal Bhuyan and Justice Atul S. Chandurkar declared the arrest of Jaskaranjit Singh, the Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD)-affiliated in-charge of the Mullanpur Dakha constituency, illegal. Singh was arrested in connection with allegations of sexual assault of a minor. The apex court held the arrest illegal because the grounds of Singh’s arrest had not been furnished to him.
The Supreme Court held that disciplinary proceedings should be initiated against the police officer who arrested a person without furnishing the grounds of arrest in writing.

In 2020, the Patna High Court censured the police for arresting and humiliating a woman doctor in an alleged case of medical negligence, reportedly without conducting any preliminary investigation or enquiry.

Hearing the doctor’s plea against the arrest, allegedly made without following proper procedure and ignoring the guidelines laid down by the Supreme Court in cases such as _Yogendra Kumar v. State of U.P._, the Court questioned the urgency behind her arrest.
The Court also pointed out that there was no serious allegation against her and asked why there had been a need to handcuff a woman doctor and take her away in a police vehicle.

India is in the midst of an unprecedented food safety crackdown, including nationwide raids against eateries, amid concern over poor hygiene and standards. The government's plan for front-of-pack red warning labels came after heated public debate on the lack of such measures.

Under an earlier plan, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India would have mandated warnings only when two ingredients breached thresholds. That plan was criticised by activists and health experts as being too lenient, prompting the Supreme Court of India to question the approach.
Warning labels will now be rolled out in a single phase, the FSSAI told the Supreme Court in a filing dated Wednesday, which is not public but was seen by _Reuters_.

"FSSAI proposes to adopt a single-phase approach ... Furthermore, where only one nutrient of concern is present, the corresponding nutrient shall be indicated in the hexagon," the court filing said, referring to the red warning symbol.
## Timelines, sweetener warnings

Sharing timelines for the first time, the FSSAI said it will issue and finalise the labelling regulations in around four months, but the industry will then get one year to mandatorily implement stricter labelling.
"There shall be voluntary implementation period of 365 days," FSSAI said.

India's food and drinks market is one of the fastest-growing for foreign players including Nestle, Unilever, Mondelez and Mars, whose food products compete in a thriving industry that includes big Indian firms.

In a newly proposed measure, the FSSAI also said any food product, including beverages, containing artificial sweeteners should carry a warning statement -- "CONTAIN NON CALORIC SWEETENER" -- on the front of packs, instead of on the back panel as currently mandated.

The nationwide debate on food safety has intensified since Reuters reported last month that India's government opted for a weaker labelling regime after lobbying by Coca-Cola and groups backing Nestle and PepsiCo which argued warning labels were ineffective. Many companies, however, have implemented such measures voluntarily in European markets.
Indians are known for their sweet tooth, and industry executives say many traditional sweets, along with products such as chips and cola, could be labelled red under the new rules.

The All India Food Processors' Association, which represents global and local firms, has told the Supreme Court that many popular products risk being covered in warnings, which will tarnish the image of Indian food globally.

The **Election Commission of India (ECI)** has rejected reports alleging that major decisions were taken without the knowledge or approval of all Election Commissioners. The Commission said its decisions have been made according to established laws, rules and procedures.

The response came after a report by _The Indian Express_ claimed that two of the three Election Commissioners had raised objections at least **14 times over a period of 10 months**. According to the report, the objections concerned several important decisions taken by the poll body.

The ECI said that presenting selected internal notes or observations without the full context could give the public only **one side of the decision-making process**. The Commission said internal discussions naturally include questions, suggestions and different views before a final decision is reached.

The Commission also stated that it functions as a **multi-member constitutional body**. According to the ECI, written observations and suggestions from its members are part of the normal process of reviewing decisions and ensuring that actions comply with legal requirements.

Addressing reports related to the **Special Intensive Revision (SIR)** of electoral rolls, the ECI said that the decisions concerning the process were taken unanimously and approved by all members. It rejected suggestions that such decisions were made without the knowledge of other commissioners.

The Commission further said that differences of opinion during internal discussions should not automatically be viewed as evidence of a dispute within the institution. Members and officials are permitted to raise concerns or make suggestions when they believe changes could improve the electoral system.

The ECI pointed to several decisions, new initiatives and electoral reforms implemented during the past year as examples of its ongoing work. It said that official orders and administrative directions are issued through established procedures and within the legal framework provided by the **2023 Act** governing the appointment and functioning of the Election Commission.

The Commission also responded to concerns regarding the security of its digital systems. It said platforms such as **ECINet** are protected by data-security protocols designed to prevent unauthorized access, changes or manipulation of information.

On voter registration and deletion of names from electoral rolls, the ECI clarified that statutory authorities such as **Electoral Registration Officers (EROs)** and **District Election Officers (DEOs)** carry out these responsibilities under the relevant legal provisions.

The Commission maintained that its internal review process includes checks and opportunities for members to express their views before decisions are finalized. It said that individual notes or observations should therefore be considered as part of the broader decision-making process rather than as complete evidence of how a final decision was reached.

The dispute comes amid wider discussions about the independence and functioning of India’s election machinery. The ECI’s statement seeks to clarify its position and says that its decisions continue to follow the applicable constitutional and legal framework.
